input: Refrigeration at a food plant uses 2365 MWh of electricity per year, and a heat-recovery retrofit has been put forward as a means of reducing that consumption. The equipment vendor projects that the retrofit would save 12% of the annual use, which corresponds to a derived saving of 284 MWh per year at the vendor figure. The capital cost is $514k. At an electricity price of $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving amounts to $34k, giving a derived simple payback of 15.1 years. It should be noted, however, that the saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant, and refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled. In light of these uncertainties, a metered trial on one of the 3 refrigeration lines is recommended before any capital decision is taken. The plant engineer owns the trial and will report its findings. The length of the payback underlines why a trial is attractive in this case: committing the full capital sum on the strength of a projection alone would expose the plant to a long recovery period if the saving turned out to be smaller than expected in practice. A metered trial, by contrast, tests the central assumption directly and at a fraction of the cost, and it produces evidence from the plant's own lines under the plant's own operating conditions, which is the evidence a capital decision of this kind ought properly to rest on.
target: Before any capital decision, a metered trial on one of the 3 refrigeration lines is recommended; the plant engineer owns the trial. The food plant uses 2365 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected by the equipment vendor to save 12% of that use. At the vendor figure, the saving is derived as 284 MWh per year. Capital cost is $514k. At an electricity price of $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $34k and the derived simple payback is 15.1 years. The saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant. Refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled, and the payback inherits that gap: the annual use averages the year, and a load concentrated in the peak month would change the hours over which recovered heat can be used. The trial meters one line through a full production cycle and compares metered use with the same line's earlier use at matched output. A capital case built on the projection alone would carry the vendor figure as its central number; the trial replaces that figure with a measured one. The payback is long at the stated price, and the trial is the step that tests whether the plant's own figure supports it. Metering a single line also separates the retrofit's effect from movements in output and product mix, which a whole-plant comparison would gather into one figure. A measured saving near the projection would give the capital case a plant figure in place of a vendor figure; a measured saving well below it would close the case at the trial's cost rather than the retrofit's, and either outcome is cheaper to learn before the capital is committed.
